text: Every supervised model has a life in two acts. First it's trained: shown many labeled examples, adjusting its internal numbers until its predictions get close to the right answers. Then it's used for inference: fed a brand-new input and asked to produce an output, with those numbers now frozen.
Training is slow and happens rarely. Inference is fast and happens constantly, every single time the model is actually used.

Underneath, a model is just a set of numbers called parameters. Training repeats one loop: run an example through the model, compare the prediction to the known label, measure how wrong it was, and nudge the parameters a little less wrong. Do that over millions of examples, many passes each, and that's why training a large model can take days or weeks on racks of GPUs.

Once training stops, the parameters are frozen and saved. Inference is just one forward pass with those fixed numbers — no comparison to a correct answer, no adjusting anything, and usually no labels at all, because the whole point is you don't already know the answer. That's why a single inference call can run in milliseconds.
So the two phases trade off completely differently: heavy compute versus milliseconds, rare versus constant, labeled data required versus none needed.

Every time you call an LLM API, you're doing pure inference — the model was trained once, already, at enormous cost, and your request is just one more forward pass through an already-finished model. Next, we'll look at exactly what goes into that input and that answer: features and labels.
